title: When compression makes it bigger
hook: Squeezing a picture should make it smaller. Can it ever make it bigger?

knows: reading a row of black and white squares
doesNotKnow: that a compression scheme can make some inputs bigger

objective: The learner can explain that run-length coding shrinks rows with long runs (16 white pixels become 16W, 3 characters) and doubles rows without runs (BWBWBWBW becomes 16 characters), and that no lossless scheme shrinks every input.

claims.text: Coded count-then-letter, BWBWBWBW becomes 1B1W1B1W1B1W1B1W: 16 characters for 8 pixels, twice as long.
claims.source: Demo.tsx encode('BWBWBWBW'); builder also ran a regex run-length coder in Node: '1B1W1B1W1B1W1B1W', length 16.
Demo.tsx encode('W' x 16) = '16W' (builder ran in Node).

claims.text: With no runs, every pixel costs a count and a letter, so the code is twice the length of the row.
claims.source: Each run of length 1 encodes as '1' plus a letter: 2 characters per pixel.

claims.text: No lossless scheme can shrink every input: there are fewer short codes than inputs, so if some get shorter, others must get longer.
claims.source: Counting (pigeonhole) argument: 2^n strings of length n but only 2^n - 1 strings shorter than n. Sayood, Introduction to Data Compression, 4th ed., ch. 1; MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms (2003), 4.1 / exercise 4.12-style argument. · Fact-check 2026-10-13: Strictly, "others must get longer" needs the code to decode every input length; for same-length rows alone some can shrink without others growing. Standard result as stated for lossless compression; acceptable.

recall.question: A compressor shrinks every photo you test it on. Your friend says it must shrink every possible file. Is that right?
options: Yes, a good compressor shrinks everything
No, some possible files must come out the same size or bigger
Yes, as long as it is lossless
recall.why: There are fewer short outputs than possible inputs, so a lossless compressor that shrinks some files must grow others, just as run-length coding doubles a row with no runs.
